# Disorders of the visual pathway

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Retina and vision > Disorders of the visual pathway*

[Original Article Link](/library/FO0g8T)

---

## Summary

The <u>visual pathway</u> transmits signals from the <u>retina</u> to the <u>visual cortex</u>. It consists of the <u>retina</u>, <u>optic nerve</u>, <u>optic chiasm</u>, <u>optic tract</u>, <u>lateral geniculate nucleus</u>, <u>optic radiations</u>, and <u>visual cortex</u>. Lesions of the <u>visual pathway</u> may lead to visual disturbances or visual loss, the pattern of which can help determine the exact location of the lesion. Unilateral <u>visual field</u> loss indicates a prechiasmal pathology, while bilateral <u>visual field</u> loss indicates a systemic, chiasmal, or retrochiasmal pathology. <u>Retinal diseases</u> mostly cause central or paracentral <u>scotomas</u>. Prechiasmal damage to the <u>visual pathway</u> usually involves the <u>optic nerve</u> (e.g., <u>optic neuritis</u>, <u>optic atrophy</u>, <u>AION</u>, <u>papilledema</u>) and may manifest with <u>anopia</u> or a <u>centrocecal scotoma</u>. Damage in the region of the <u>optic chiasm</u> is most commonly due to compression by a <u>pituitary adenoma</u> or <u>craniopharyngioma</u> and manifests with <u>bitemporal heteronymous hemianopsia</u> (lesions of the crossing fibers) or <u>binasal hemianopsia</u> (lesions of noncrossing fibers). Retrochiasmal <u>visual pathway</u> damage occurs in the region of the <u>optic tract</u>, <u>lateral geniculate nucleus</u>, <u>optic radiation</u>, or <u>visual cortex</u> and is most commonly due to cerebral <u>ischemia</u> or hemorrhage, tumors, or trauma. It usually manifests with <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u> or homonymous <u>quadrantanopsia</u>.

---

## Overview of the visual pathways

The <u>visual pathways</u> transmit signals from the <u>retina</u> to the <u>visual cortex</u> (<u>striate cortex</u>, <u>brodmann area 17</u>).




| Overview |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Characteristics | <br>Lesions<br> | Causes |
| <u>Retina</u> | <br>* <u>Cones</u> and rods transform light into visual signals, which are projected to the <u>brain</u> via the <u>optic nerve</u>.<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Central scotoma</u> occurs in case of <u>macula</u> involvement<br><br>* <u>Paracentral scotoma</u><br><br>* Occurs in case of <u>macula</u> involvement with foveal sparing (e.g., <u>hydroxychloroquine</u>/<u>chloroquine maculopathy</u>)<br><br>* Seen as concentric rings of <u>hypopigmentation</u> and <u>hyperpigmentation</u> on the <u>macula</u> (“<u>bull's eye maculopathy</u>”)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Diseases of the retina</u><br><br>* <u>Retinal detachment</u><br><br>* <u>Retinal vessel occlusion</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Optic nerve</u> | <br><br>* Transmits visual information from the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>retina</u> to the <u>brain</u><br><br>* Afferent limb of <u>pupillary reflex</u> and <u>accommodation reflex</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> blindness (<u>anopia</u>), <u>scotoma</u><br><br>* <u>Centrocecal scotoma</u>: loss of <u>vision</u> in the <u>fovea centralis</u> region and a <u>blind spot</u><br><br>* <u>Pupillary light reflex</u>: loss of afferent limb → absent <u>direct pupillary light reflex</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Optic neuritis</u> (MS)<br><br>* <u>Optic atrophy</u><br><br>* <u>Retinal vessel occlusion</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy</u><br><br>* <u>Traumatic optic neuropathy</u> (<u>TON</u>)<br><br>* <u>Papilledema</u><br><br><br> |
| Optic chiasm | <br><br>* Fibers from nasal part of the <u>retina</u>  cross to <u>contralateral</u> side<br><br>* Fibers from the temporal part of the <u>retina</u>  do not cross to the <u>contralateral</u> side<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Middle lesions (crossing fibers) → <u>bitemporal heteronymous hemianopsia</u><br><br>* Bilateral lesions (non-crossing fibers) → <u>binasal hemianopsia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pituitary adenoma</u><br><br>* <u>Craniopharyngioma</u><br><br>* Parasellar <u>aneurysm</u> of the <u>internal carotid artery</u><br><br>* <u>Meningioma</u><br><br><br> |
| Optic tract | <br><br>* Transmits information of the<br><br>* <u>ipsilateral</u>, nasal <u>visual field</u><br><br>* <u>contralateral</u>, temporal <u>visual field</u><br><br>* Projects to <u>lateral geniculate nucleus</u>, <u>pretectal area</u>, <u>superior colliculi</u>, <u>suprachiasmatic nuclei</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Middle cerebral artery</u> (<u>MCA</u>) <u>infarction</u><br><br> |
| <u>Lateral geniculate nucleus</u> (<u>LGN</u>) | <br><br>* Transmits information of the<br><br>* <u>ipsilateral</u>, nasal <u>visual field</u><br><br>* <u>contralateral</u>, temporal <u>visual field</u><br><br>* Projects to <u>primary visual cortex</u> via <u>optic radiations</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Infarction</u> of either the <u>MCA</u> or PCA [[1]](/library/czXa700)<br><br>* Sometimes <u>MCA</u> → <u>anterior choroidal artery</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior cerebral artery</u> → <u>lateral</u> choroidal <u>artery</u><br><br> |
| <u>Optic radiations</u> | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>/<u>lateral</u> bundle in <u>Meyer loop</u> <br><br>* Passes through the <u>temporal lobe</u> in close proximity to the inferior horn of the <u>lateral ventricle</u><br><br>* Transmits information of the superior <u>visual field</u> from the lower <u>retina</u><br><br>* Projects to the lingual <u>gyrus</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>/<u>medial</u> bundle<br><br>* Located in the <u>parietal lobe</u>, passes through the <u>internal capsule</u><br><br>* Transmits information of the inferior <u>visual field</u> from the upper <u>retina</u><br><br>* Projects to the cuneus <u>gyrus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* More common than <u>optic tract</u> or <u>LGN</u> lesions<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>/<u>lateral</u>/inferior bundle (<u>Meyer loop</u>)<br>* <u>Contralateral</u> upper homonymous <u>quadrantanopsia</u> (“pie in the sky”)<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>/<u>medial</u>/superior bundle<br>* <u>Contralateral</u> lower homonymous <u>quadrantanopsia</u> (“pie on the floor”)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>MCA</u> <u>infarction</u><br><br>* Upper <u>quadrantanopsia</u> indicates <u>temporal lobe</u> lesion<br><br>* Lower <u>quadrantanopsia</u> indicates <u>parietal lobe</u> lesion<br><br><br> |
| <u>Visual cortex</u> | <br>* Located in the <u>calcarine sulcus</u> of the <u>occipital lobe</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u> with <u>macular sparing</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior cerebral artery</u> (PCA) <u>infarction</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Unilateral <u>visual field</u> loss → pathology mainly in front of the <u>optic chiasm</u>. Bilateral <u>visual field</u> loss → pathology mainly in or behind the <u>optic chiasm</u>




> [!NOTE]
> Remember that the Meyer Loop transmits the signal from the Lower <u>retina</u>, Looping around the inferior horn of the Lateral ventricle.

## Scotoma and anopia

### Scotoma




An area within an otherwise normal <u>visual field</u> where <u>vision</u> is temporarily or permanently reduced or absent




* Blind spot: a physiologic <u>scotoma</u> in the <u>visual field</u> formed by <u>axons</u> leaving the <u>eye</u> to form the <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>optic papilla</u>) temporal to the center of the <u>visual field</u>

* Central scotoma: <u>scotoma</u> in the center of an <u>eye</u>'s <u>visual field</u>

* Paracentral scotoma: <u>scotoma</u> near the center of an <u>eye</u>'s <u>visual field</u>

* Centrocecal scotoma: <u>scotoma</u> running from the center to the <u>blind spot</u> of an <u>eye</u>'s <u>visual field</u>

* Arcuate scotoma: an arc-shaped <u>scotoma</u> that starts at the <u>blind spot</u> and courses over the center of an <u>eye</u>'s <u>visual field</u>

* Scintillating scotoma: an arch-shaped <u>scotoma</u> that starts centrally and shifts peripherally, that is typically experienced during an <u>migraine aura</u> (especially in retinal <u>migraines</u>)

* Perception of an arch-shaped area of decreased <u>vision</u>

* Moves from paracentral to peripheral <u>vision</u>

* Flickering lights appearing in zigzag patterns

* Usually bilateral

* Typically lasts for 15–30 min [[3]](/library/2FXTh-)

* May be followed by <u>headache</u> or, less commonly, occur concomitantly with <u>headache</u>.

* See “<u>Migraine</u>” for more information about diagnostics and treatment.





![Types of scotoma](media/k0jurgoadzfrztikk5h84xa2.jpg)

Types of scotoma

![Bilateral central scotoma in perimetry](media/pzvm0ze9bcbsasvvtj5oub7d.jpg)

Bilateral central scotoma in perimetry

![Bjerrum scotoma](media/yym2haa1ekc2kuj2o8oqx128.jpg)

Bjerrum scotoma




### Anopia




A larger <u>visual field</u> defect that affects a quarter, half, or the entire <u>vision</u> of an <u>eye</u>




* Unilateral anopia: <u>vision loss</u> in one <u>eye</u>

* Hemianopia: <u>vision loss</u> in one half of the <u>visual field</u> separated by the vertical midline

* Bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia: <u>vision loss</u> at the outer (temporal) half of the <u>visual field</u> of both eyes

* Binasal hemianopia: <u>vision loss</u> at the inner (nasal) half of the <u>visual field</u> of both eyes

* Homonymous hemianopia: <u>vision loss</u> of one half of the <u>visual field</u> on the same side in both eyes (e.g., right <u>homonymous hemianopia</u> is a <u>vision loss</u> in the temporal <u>visual field</u> of the right <u>eye</u> and the nasal <u>visual field</u> of the left <u>eye</u>)

* Macular sparing: macular <u>vision</u> is preserved despite adjacent <u>visual field</u> loss

* Quadrantanopia: <u>vision loss</u> in a quarter of the <u>visual field</u> of both eyes





> [!NOTE]
> Unilateral <u>vision</u> field loss indicates a disorder of a structure <u>anterior</u> to the <u>optic chiasm</u>. Bilateral <u>visual field</u> loss indicates a pathology at or <u>posterior</u> to the <u>optic chiasm</u>.

## Prechiasmal visual pathway damage

Prechiasmal damage to the <u>visual pathway</u> mainly involves the <u>optic nerve</u>. For <u>retinal diseases</u>, see “<u>Diseases of the retina</u>.”

---

## Optic neuritis

### Definition [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)




<u>Optic neuritis</u> is inflammation of the <u>optic nerve</u>; subtypes include <u>retrobulbar neuritis</u> and <u>papillitis</u>.




* Retrobulbar neuritis: inflammation of the retrobulbar part of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* <u>Papillitis</u>: inflammation of the <u>optic disc</u>





![Papillitis in optic neuritis](media/x3oxwsvbffgvn7jxuvb7aybw.jpg)

Papillitis in optic neuritis




### Etiology [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[5]](/library/-xWD_n0)




* Most common cause: <u>multiple sclerosis</u> (MS)  [[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)

* Infections (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>syphilis</u>, <u>Lyme disease</u>, viral infections)

* <u>Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders</u>

* Other inflammatory and autoimmune conditions (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>)

* <u>Idiopathic</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Multiple sclerosis</u> is the most common cause of <u>optic neuritis</u>. [[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)




### Clinical features [[5]](/library/-xWD_n0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Vision</u> impairment: reduced <u>visual acuity</u>, subacute <u>vision loss</u>, <u>dyschromatopsia</u>, <u>visual field</u> defects (e.g., <u>central scotoma</u>)

* Retrobulbar <u>pain</u> (increases with <u>eye movements</u>)

* Typically monocular





> [!TIP]
> <u>Optic neuritis</u> typically manifests with unilateral, subacute <u>vision loss</u> and orbital <u>pain</u> that worsens with <u>eye movements</u>. [[5]](/library/-xWD_n0)




### Diagnostics [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)




<u>Optic neuritis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.




* <u>Physical examination</u> and <u>examination of the eye</u>

* <u>Swinging-flashlight test</u>: <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u> [[8]](/library/0BWezn0)

* <u>Ophthalmoscopy</u>  

* <u>Retrobulbar neuritis</u>: may be normal

* <u>Papillitis</u>: may show inflammatory changes (e.g., poorly defined <u>papilla</u> and <u>hyperemia</u>)

* <u>Visual acuity testing</u>

* <u>Color vision</u> testing, e.g., assessing for <u>red desaturation</u>

* <u>Neurological examination</u>

* Confirmatory studies and evaluation for the underlying cause

* <u>MRI</u> head and <u>orbits</u> with and without IV contrast (first-line studies)  [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[9]](/library/RU1l1T0)

* <u>CSF analysis</u>: Findings may indicate the underlying cause, e.g., <u>oligoclonal bands</u> in MS.

* <u>Serology</u> (e.g., <u>Lyme serology</u>, <u>antinuclear antibodies</u>): obtained in consultation with specialists to assess for infectious and autoimmune etiologies

* See also “<u>Multiple sclerosis</u>” and “<u>Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders</u>.”

* Specialist diagnostics

* <u>Optical coherence tomography</u>: can show subtle changes in the <u>retina</u> and <u>optic disc</u>

* <u>Visual evoked potential</u> (<u>VEP</u>)

* Used to assess for conduction disorders of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* <u>VEP</u> cannot be used to differentiate between etiologies of <u>optic neuritis</u>. [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)





![Papillitis in optic neuritis](media/x3oxwsvbffgvn7jxuvb7aybw.jpg)

Papillitis in optic neuritis




### Treatment [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)[[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Although many patients experience symptom improvement without treatment, research has shown that treatment reduces recovery times and may improve outcomes. [[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)




* Consult <u>neurology</u> and consider inpatient admission.

* Begin high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>, e.g.:

* IV <u>methylprednisolone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 3–7 days [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)

* Followed by oral <u>prednisone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 11–14 days [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)[[6]](/library/ZBWZzn0)

* Depending on the underlying cause, advanced treatment modalities (e.g., <u>plasmapheresis</u> and <u>intravenous immunoglobulin</u>) may be used.

* Manage the underlying condition in consultation with specialists, e.g., for <u>treatment of MS</u> or <u>treatment of Lyme disease</u>.





### Prognosis [[4]](/library/aBWQzn0)




* Prognosis depends on the underlying etiology.

* <u>Visual acuity</u> typically starts improving within weeks.

* Some degree of impairment often persists.

---

## Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION)

* Definition: segmental or generalized <u>infarction</u> of the <u>anterior</u> part of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Etiology

* Nonarteritic form due to <u>atherosclerosis</u> (NAION)

* Arteritic form due to <u>giant cell arteritis</u> (AAION)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* NAION: peak <u>incidence</u> between 50 and 70 years of age, but also observed in younger patients

* AAION: almost always after 60 years of age

* Clinical features

* Sudden unilateral loss of <u>vision</u>

* Wedge-shaped and altitudinal <u>visual field</u> defects

* AAION: other <u>symptoms of giant cell arteritis</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>

* Acute: <u>edematous</u>, poorly defined <u>optic disc</u>, usually sectoral; pale or <u>hyperemic</u>; radial hemorrhage around the disc margin

* Late course of the disease: <u>optic atrophy</u>

* Laboratory findings

* AAION: ↑ <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* NAION: normal <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* AAION: <u>temporal artery biopsy</u>

* Treatment

* AAION: immediate high-dose systemic <u>glucocorticoids</u>

* NAION: trial of hemodilution and <u>systemic glucocorticoid</u> therapy

* Prognosis

* Typically poor: permanent loss of <u>vision</u>

* Involvement of the other <u>eye</u> is common during the course of the disease.





> [!TIP]
> Immediate high-dose <u>glucocorticoid</u> treatment is essential in AAION.

---

## Traumatic optic neuropathy (TON)

* Definition: <u>vision loss</u> due to injury of the <u>optic nerve</u> from a penetrating or <u>blunt force head trauma</u>

* Etiology

* <u>Blunt force head trauma</u> (most common), e.g., due to motorcycle and bicycle collisions, <u>sports injuries</u>, physical assault

* Penetrating orbital trauma, e.g., <u>stab wound</u>

* Pathophysiology [[10]](/library/PE1WDi0)

* Indirect <u>TON</u>: blunt force head trauma → force transmitted to the <u>optic canal</u> through <u>cranial</u> bones → swelling and <u>ischemia</u> within the optic canal → <u>contusion</u> of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Direct <u>TON</u>: <u>penetrating trauma</u> (e.g., orbital and/or facial <u>fracture</u>) → bone fragments and/or hemorrhage within the optic canal → transection or avulsion of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Clinical features

* Findings consistent with

* Recent <u>head trauma</u> (e.g., <u>headache</u>, <u>nausea</u>)

* Sudden unilateral <u>vision</u> impairment (e.g., blurry <u>vision</u>, sudden <u>vision loss</u>, <u>color blindness</u>, <u>central scotoma</u>)

* <u>Physical examination</u>: signs of orbital trauma and/or <u>fracture</u> (e.g., <u>ecchymosis</u>, <u>hematoma</u>, and/or <u>edema</u> of <u>soft tissues</u>)

* Diagnostics: All patients with suspected <u>TON</u> require <u>fundoscopy</u>, a <u>CT scan</u> of the head, and an ophthalmological examination to assess <u>visual acuity</u>, <u>visual fields</u>, and <u>pupillary reflex</u>.

* <u>Swinging-flashlight</u> test: <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u>

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>

* Indirect <u>TON</u>

* Initially normal findings

* <u>Optic atrophy</u> may be present 3–6 weeks after injury. [[10]](/library/PE1WDi0)

* Direct <u>TON</u>: <u>optic disc</u> swelling and hemorrhage

* <u>CT scan</u> of the head: <u>optic canal</u> <u>fracture</u>, <u>optic nerve</u> <u>hematoma</u>, and/or bony fragment

* Treatment [[11]](/library/ZE1Z8i0)

* Observation for mild symptoms

* <u>Corticosteroids</u> and/or surgical decompression of the <u>optic nerve</u>

---

## Toxic-metabolic optic neuropathy

### Definition [[12]](/library/1BW2-n0)[[13]](/library/cBWa-n0)




<u>Toxic-metabolic optic neuropathy</u> is damage to the <u>optic nerve</u> caused by toxins and/or nutritional deficiencies.




### Etiology [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[12]](/library/1BW2-n0)[[13]](/library/cBWa-n0)[[14]](/library/hYdcKo0)




* <u>Methanol poisoning</u>

* Nutritional deficiencies, e.g., <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>

* Drug-induced, e.g., <u>ethambutol</u>, <u>aminoglycosides</u>, <u>barbiturates</u>, <u>linezolid</u>, <u>infliximab</u>





### Clinical features [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[12]](/library/1BW2-n0)[[13]](/library/cBWa-n0)




* Reduced <u>visual acuity</u>, <u>dyschromatopsia</u>, and <u>visual field</u> defects (commonly <u>central scotoma</u>)

* Typically bilateral, progressive, and painless





### Diagnostics [[12]](/library/1BW2-n0)[[13]](/library/cBWa-n0)




* <u>Focused toxicological history and physical examination</u>

* <u>Examination of the eye</u>

* <u>Swinging-flashlight test</u>: no <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u>

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>: often initially normal; swollen disc and/or <u>hyperemia</u> may be seen

* <u>Visual field examination</u>: <u>central scotoma</u>

* <u>MRI</u> head and <u>orbits</u> to exclude compressive lesions

* Additional diagnostics depending on the suspected etiology (e.g., serum <u>methanol</u> levels in suspected <u>methanol poisoning</u>)

* Assessment of <u>nutritional status</u>, including <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> and <u>folate</u> levels





### Treatment [[12]](/library/1BW2-n0)[[13]](/library/cBWa-n0)




* Management of the underlying cause, e.g., discontinuation of the causative drug, management of <u>toxic alcohol poisoning</u>

* For a comprehensive approach to <u>poisoning</u>, see “<u>Approach to the poisoned patient</u>.”

---

## Papilledema

### Definition [[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)[[16]](/library/dBWo-n0)




<u>Papilledema</u> is swelling of the <u>optic disc</u> due to <u>elevated intracranial pressure</u> (<u>ICP</u>).




### Etiology [[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)[[16]](/library/dBWo-n0)




* <u>Hypertensive encephalopathy</u> due to <u>hypertensive emergency</u>

* <u>Idiopathic intracranial hypertension</u> (<u>pseudotumor cerebri</u>)

* Space-occupying lesions: <u>intracranial tumors</u> (e.g., <u>medulloblastoma</u>), <u>cerebral abscess</u>

* <u>Hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Drug-induced intracranial hypertension</u> (e.g., due to <u>hypervitaminosis A</u>)

* <u>Venous sinus thrombosis</u>

* See also “<u>Causes of elevated ICP</u>.”





### Pathophysiology




Increased <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> pressure disrupts the axoplasmic flow in the <u>optic nerve</u>. [[17]](/library/1O12rS0)




### Clinical features [[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)[[16]](/library/dBWo-n0)




* Acute

* The most common symptom is <u>headache</u>. [[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)

* Visual impairment is typically minimal; transient blurry <u>vision</u> or loss of <u>vision</u> may occur.

* Other <u>signs of elevated ICP</u> may be present (e.g., <u>nausea and vomiting</u>).

* Chronic (rare): impaired <u>vision</u>, <u>visual field</u> defects, and blindness





### Diagnostics [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)[[16]](/library/dBWo-n0)




* <u>Visual field examination</u>:  <u>arcuate scotoma</u>, widened <u>blind spot</u>

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>

* Acute  

* <u>Edematous</u>, poorly defined, prominent <u>optic disc</u> with blurry margins

* Radial hemorrhage around the disc margin

* Later stages of disease: <u>Optic atrophy</u> may be present.

* <u>Diagnostics for elevated ICP</u>: CT or <u>MRI</u> head

* Once other <u>causes of elevated ICP</u> have been ruled out: Obtain <u>diagnostics for IIH</u> (e.g., <u>lumbar puncture</u>).





![Optic disc edema](media/uhxcvfgt8nz6ujdizfvo5o19.jpg)

Optic disc edema

![Bilateral optic disc edema](media/law2dslfqtga9udfv1ms3t0h.jpg)

Bilateral optic disc edema




### Treatment [[7]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[15]](/library/WBWP-n0)[[16]](/library/dBWo-n0)




* Initiate <u>management of elevated ICP</u> immediately.

* Further treatment focuses on the underlying cause, e.g., <u>management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension</u>, <u>management of hypertensive emergencies</u>.

## Damage in the region of the optic chiasm

* Etiology

* Most commonly: compression by <u>pituitary adenoma</u> (<u>prolactinoma</u>), <u>craniopharyngioma</u>, <u>meningioma</u>, <u>aneurysms</u> of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>

* <u>Demyelination</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>

* Trauma

* Pathophysiology

* <u>Medial</u> lesion (e.g., <u>pituitary adenoma</u>) → temporal <u>visual field</u> defects

* <u>Lateral</u> lesion (e.g., <u>aneurysm</u> of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>) → nasal <u>visual field</u> defects

* Clinical features

* <u>Visual field</u> defects/impaired <u>vision</u>: most commonly <u>bitemporal heteronymous hemianopsia</u>

* Sometimes chiasmal syndrome: triad of bitemporal <u>visual field</u> defects, unilateral or bilateral reduction in <u>visual acuity</u>, and <u>optic atrophy</u>

* Treatment
* Depending on the cause

* Neurosurgical

* Pharmacological

* Prognosis: Complete regression of impaired <u>vision</u>/<u>visual field</u> defects is possible with timely treatment.

## Retrochiasmal visual pathway damage

* Definition: damage in the region of the <u>optic tract</u>, <u>lateral geniculate nucleus</u>, <u>optic radiation</u>, or <u>visual cortex</u>

* Etiology

* Cerebral <u>ischemia</u>/hemorrhage (e.g., <u>posterior cerebral artery</u> occlusion)

* Tumors

* Trauma

* Other causes (e.g., <u>aneurysms</u> of the <u>posterior communicating artery</u>, <u>abscesses</u>, <u>meningitis</u>, vasospasms)

* Clinical features

* <u>Visual field</u> defects/impaired <u>vision</u>: most commonly <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u> and homonymous <u>quadrantanopsia</u>

* <u>Optic atrophy</u> in cases with a <u>CN III</u> lesion

* Diagnostics

* <u>Perimetry</u>

* Imaging: CT, <u>MRI</u>

* Prognosis: usually no regression of <u>visual field</u> defects
